title: James, Peter & Jude
tagline: Four short letters — on faith that works, hope under suffering, growing knowledge and contending for the faith — three of which the early church long disputed.

intro.text: Four short letters stand together near the end of the New Testament: one from James, two under Peter's name and one from Jude. Athanasius, listing the books of the New Testament in 367, grouped them with the three letters of John as the seven Catholic letters — that is, the general letters.

Only 1 Peter was accepted everywhere from the beginning. Writing in the early 300s, Eusebius still counted James, Jude and 2 Peter among the disputed books, though recognised by many; James and Jude, he noted, had been read publicly in very many churches. Before the end of that century all four stood in Athanasius's list.

Each has its own voice: James on faith that shows itself in action, 1 Peter on hope under suffering, 2 Peter on growing in knowledge while waiting for the Lord's coming, and Jude on contending for the faith against intruders. They are also bound together — James and 1 Peter share phrases, and Jude and 2 Peter share a whole run of images — and which way the borrowing went is still argued.

James was one of the brothers of Jesus named at Nazareth, and during the ministry "neither did his brethren believe in him". After the resurrection Jesus "was seen of James", and the brother who had not believed became a leader of the church in Jerusalem, one of its "pillars", as Paul says; Mayor held that he wrote the letter of James. Hegesippus remembered him as James "the Just"; in about AD 62 the high priest Ananus had him stoned, and Josephus calls him "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ".

Peter was born Simon, a fisherman of Bethsaida, and his brother Andrew brought him to Jesus, who named him Cephas, "A stone" — Peter in Greek. He became the spokesman of the Twelve and confessed Jesus as "the Christ, the Son of the living God", yet denied him three times on the night of the arrest; the risen Lord restored him: "Feed my sheep". Eusebius records that he was crucified at Rome under Nero, though the ISBE notes his Rome visit "is only tradition and nothing more".

Jude — "Juda" in Mark, "Judas" in Matthew — was another of Jesus' brothers, probably the youngest or the youngest but one, Mayor thought, and like the others he came to faith after the resurrection. The letter's writer calls himself only "the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James": Mayor, Bigg and the ISBE take him to be this brother; Easton, the apostle Judas. Hegesippus tells how Jude's grandsons, brought before the emperor Domitian as heirs of David, showed hands hardened by farm work and said Christ's kingdom was "not a temporal nor an earthly kingdom".

author.text: The writer calls himself only "James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ" and claims no title. Three men of that name appear in the New Testament. James the son of Zebedee was put to death early, which is why most writers rule him out; the views that remain connect the letter with James "the Lord's brother", leader of the church in Jerusalem, though they differ over who he was and whether he wrote it. Mayor noticed wording shared with James's speech and letter in Acts 15: the letter-opening "greeting" appears in the New Testament only here, in the Jerusalem letter of Acts 15:23, and in a Roman officer's letter at Acts 23:26.

recipients.text: "The twelve tribes which are scattered abroad" — literally "in the dispersion", the word for Jews living outside the land. They call Abraham "our father", and their meeting is a "synagogue" (the KJV's "assembly" at 2:2), the only place in the New Testament where that word names a Christian gathering. Mayor took them to be Jewish Christians of the eastern dispersion; the ISBE, Jews of the dispersion generally, most of them in Syria and Asia Minor.

writtenFrom.text: The letter does not say. Mayor, Schaff and Easton place it in Jerusalem, pointing to its pictures of the land: the early and latter rain, the scorching wind that withers the grass, figs, olives and vines.

date.text: Disputed. Mayor, with many others listed in the ISBE, put it in the 40s AD, before the Jerusalem council of about 51 — which would make it perhaps the oldest writing in the New Testament — because it has no Gentile question and no debate over circumcision. Others place it late in James's life, about 60–62 (Easton among them). A third group, including Baur and Harnack, dated it after his death, between about 70 and 150.

occasion.text: The readers are meeting trials of many kinds. In their gatherings they favour the rich; they talk about faith without living it; their speech runs out of control; they quarrel out of worldly ambition; rich landowners cheat the labourers who reap their fields; and patience is wearing thin. The letter ends with no greetings at all, only a charge to bring back anyone who wanders from the truth.

themes.text: Trials and endurance. Testing ripens faith into endurance; "patience" comes three times and "be patient" three more, with the farmer, the prophets and Job held up as patterns.
Wisdom from above. Wisdom is asked of a generous God, and true wisdom is known by a peaceable, gentle life, unlike the jealous "wisdom" from below.
Hearing and doing. "Doer" comes four times in James; in the rest of the New Testament the word is used only twice.
Faith shown by works. "Faith" comes 16 times and "works" 15, most of them packed into 2:14–26: faith that does nothing is dead.
Rich and poor. God has chosen the poor; the rich fade like a flower, and those who hold back wages will answer for it.
The tongue. A small member that steers the whole body like a bit or a rudder, and can set a forest alight.
An undivided heart. "Double minded" (1:8 and 4:8, its only two uses in the New Testament) stands against single loyalty to God; "friendship of the world is enmity with God".
Prayer and the Lord's coming. Patience until the Lord comes, prayer in trouble and sickness, and Elijah as proof of what a righteous person's prayer can do.

A letter of commands. A hand count of the Greek text on this site finds 47 commands in James's own voice in 108 verses (by chapter 11, 4, 4, 12 and 16), plus 7 more inside quoted speech; two of the 47 are "Go to now", which grammarians often treat as an exclamation. This is a hand count, not yet checked against a grammatically tagged Greek text, and other editions of the Greek can add one or two, so published counts vary. The densest runs are 4:7–10, ten commands in four verses, and 5:7–16, thirteen.

Scripture in James. The letter leans on the Old Testament throughout — the "royal law" of loving one's neighbour, Abraham, Rahab, Job, Elijah — but one appeal, "the scripture saith" at 4:5, matches no Old Testament verse. Mayor called it "the difficult passage"; it is left unresolved here.

keyVerses.why: Trials as the place where faith learns endurance.
The open invitation to ask God for wisdom.
Every good gift comes down from an unchanging Father of lights.
The letter's call in one line: doers of the word, not hearers only.
Pure religion: care for orphans and widows, and a life kept clean.
The closing image of the faith-and-works argument.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.
What a righteous person's prayer can do.

Woe to the rich who hold back wages

author.text: "Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ", who also calls himself an elder and a witness of Christ's sufferings. He wrote "by Silvanus" — Paul's companion Silas — and passes on greetings from "Marcus my son", that is John Mark. Eusebius records that the ancient elders used the letter freely as an undisputed work. In modern times Harnack doubted that it came from a personal disciple of Jesus and thought its opening and closing verses were added later; Bigg answered him.

recipients.text: "The strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia" — sojourners far from home, spread over five regions of Asia Minor. They had once lived as the Gentiles do and "in time past were not a people", which Bigg and the ISBE take to mean they were mainly Gentile Christians; Eusebius read the address as written to Jews of the dispersion.

writtenFrom.text: "The church that is at Babylon" sends greetings — though in the Greek the words "church that is" are not there, and the KJV marks them as supplied. Whether Babylon means Rome under a figure, the city on the Euphrates, a fortress in Egypt or Jerusalem is disputed.

date.text: Disputed. Bigg put it between AD 58 and 64, before Nero's persecution; the ISBE about 64, under Nero; Mayor during Paul's imprisonment in Rome. Harnack dated it 83–93 (possibly as early as 63) and did not think Peter wrote it. Tradition has Peter die at Rome under Nero.

occasion.text: The readers are slandered as evildoers and reproached for the name of Christ; some suffer "as a Christian" — one of only three places the word appears in the New Testament. A "fiery trial" is upon them. His stated aim is to exhort them and to testify that this is the true grace of God in which they stand.

themes.text: A living hope. In the site's Greek text "hope" appears three times and the verb "to hope" twice; the ISBE calls this the letter of hope.
Suffering. The verb "suffer" comes 12 times and the noun "sufferings" 4: suffering for doing right, as Christ suffered, is the letter's steady subject.
Strangers and pilgrims. The readers are sojourners whose true home lies ahead.

Good conduct among outsiders. The word the KJV renders "conversation" — a whole way of life — appears six times, and the words for doing good another six: the answer to slander is a life that silences it.
Submission. "Submit" and "be subject" come seven times — to rulers, to masters, wives to husbands, the younger to the elder, and all to one another.
Christ the example and the living stone. "Stone" comes five times in 2:4–8; Christ's suffering is the pattern his people follow.
Grace and glory. "Grace" appears ten times and "glory" eleven — suffering now, glory to follow.

keyVerses.why: The opening praise: a living hope through the resurrection.
Redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish.
Israel's titles given to the church: a chosen generation, a royal priesthood.
Christ bore our sins in his own body; by his stripes we are healed.
Always ready to give a reason for the hope within, with meekness.
Fervent love that covers a multitude of sins.
Cast all your care on him, for he cares for you.
Be sober and watchful: the adversary prowls like a roaring lion.

outline.title: Greeting to the chosen strangers of the five provinces
Praise for a living hope and an unfading inheritance; faith tested like gold
Be holy as God is holy; redeemed by precious blood, born again by the living word
Living stones on the chosen corner stone: a royal priesthood, a people of God
Good conduct among outsiders: rulers, masters, wives and husbands, one another
Suffering for doing right; Christ's suffering, the spirits in prison, Noah and baptism
The end is near: prayer, fervent love, hospitality, gifts used as stewards
The fiery trial: sharing Christ's sufferings, suffering as a Christian
To elders and the younger: shepherd the flock, be clothed with humility
Humble yourselves, cast your care on God, resist the roaring lion
Silvanus, Babylon and Mark; the kiss of charity

Counting the related words for "well-doer" (2:14) and "well doing" (4:19).

places.note: The site's place data puts this Babylon at Rome; the city on the Euphrates is the other main candidate.

Quotation: "All flesh is as grass"; Peter ends "the word of the Lord endureth for ever".

Quotation following the Greek Old Testament: "shall not be confounded" (KJV Isaiah: "shall not make haste").
Quotation: the rejected stone becomes the head of the corner.
Quotation: a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence.

Allusion: "not my people" become the people of God.
Allusion: those who had not obtained mercy.

Allusion: with his stripes we are healed.
Allusion: like sheep gone astray.
Allusion: Sarah calls Abraham "my lord".
Quotation: he that will love life, and see good days.
Allusion: be not afraid of their terror; sanctify the Lord.
Allusion: eight souls saved in the ark.
Allusion: love covers all sins; compare Jas 5:20.
Quotation following the Greek Old Testament: "If the righteous scarcely be saved".
Quotation in the Greek Old Testament's form, as in Jas 4:6.
Allusion: cast thy burden upon the LORD.

author.text: "Simon Peter, a servant and an apostle of Jesus Christ" — many Greek manuscripts have the Hebrew form "Symeon", used of Peter elsewhere only in James's speech at Acts 15:14. The writer says the Lord has shown him his death is near, that he heard the Father's voice on "the holy mount", that this is his second letter, and he speaks of "our beloved brother Paul". It was the most doubted of the four in the early church, and its authorship is still argued.

recipients.text: Those who "have obtained like precious faith with us". If "this second epistle" points back to 1 Peter, they are the same readers. Zahn thought an earlier letter was lost and the readers were Jewish Christians; Bigg suggested Corinth; Mayor held they were not the readers of 1 Peter.

writtenFrom.text: The letter does not say. Zahn suggested Antioch; if it is Peter's last letter, tradition would place it in Rome.

date.text: Disputed. Zahn dated it about 60–63; Easton, the ISBE and Calvin put it shortly before Peter's death in the mid-60s; Chase about 150. Mayor took it to be later than the apostles and weighed several second-century dates.

occasion.text: A farewell reminder before the writer's death. False teachers will arise among the readers, marked by greed, sensuality and contempt for authority, and scoffers will ask, "Where is the promise of his coming?"

themes.text: Knowledge. In the site's Greek text "full knowledge" comes four times and "knowledge" three, and the letter ends "grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord". The ISBE puts it in a line: the key word of 1 Peter is hope, of 2 Peter knowledge.
Godliness, and a ladder of virtues. "Godliness" comes four times; to faith the readers are to add virtue, knowledge, temperance, patience, godliness, brotherly kindness and charity.
Remembering. The writer means to keep putting them in mind of what they already know, before he is gone.
Judgment kept in store. "Reserved" comes four times and "destruction" or "perdition" six: the angels, the false teachers and the present world are all kept for judgment.
The Lord's coming. A thousand years are as one day to the Lord; the delay is his patience, and the day of the Lord will come as a thief, bringing new heavens and a new earth.
Saviour. The title comes five times, always of Jesus.
A rare word. "Cast them down to hell" (2:4) renders a verb meaning "to put in Tartarus", found nowhere else in the Bible; Mayor called it "the extremely rare word".

keyVerses.why: God's power has given all that life and godliness need.
Partakers of the divine nature.
Not clever fables: eyewitnesses of his majesty.
Prophecy came as holy men were moved by the Holy Ghost.
One day with the Lord as a thousand years.
The Lord's patience: not willing that any should perish.
The hope of new heavens and a new earth.
The closing charge: grow in grace and knowledge.

God's power and promises; add to faith the seven virtues; make your calling sure
Reminders before putting off "this tabernacle"
Not fables: eyewitnesses of the transfiguration; prophecy came from God
False teachers will arise
God judges and rescues: the angels, Noah's flood, Sodom and Lot
Portrait of the false teachers: like Balaam, wells without water, the dog and the sow (from 2:10, mid-verse)
The scoffers forget the flood; the present world is kept for fire
A day as a thousand years; God is patient; the day comes as a thief
Holy living while waiting for new heavens and a new earth; Paul's letters
Guard yourselves, grow in grace and knowledge; doxology

Including "the day of the Lord" (3:10), "the day of God" (3:12) and "for ever" (3:18), literally "unto the day of eternity".

Allusion: fire on Sodom and Gomorrah.
Allusion: Lot rescued.

Allusion: the earth standing out of the water.
Allusion: the flood.
Allusion: a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday.
Allusion: new heavens and a new earth.
Allusion: new heavens and a new earth.

author.text: "Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James." He seems to stand apart from the apostles, asking his readers to remember what they foretold. Mayor, Bigg and the ISBE take him to be the brother of Jesus and of James named in Mark 6:3; Easton identifies him with the apostle "Judas of James"; others have proposed a later Judas.

recipients.text: Unnamed: "them that are sanctified by God the Father, and preserved in Jesus Christ, and called". Mayor and the ISBE suggest the same Jewish-Christian circle as James; Bigg thought we are left wholly to guesswork.

writtenFrom.text: Unknown. Egypt or Alexandria, and Palestine or Jerusalem, have been suggested; Bigg found neither convincing. Easton thought it was written apparently in Palestine.

date.text: Disputed. Bigg put it not much after 65; Easton 66 or 70; Zahn 70–75, reading verse 5 as a sign that Jerusalem had fallen; Mayor and Lumby about 80; Chase not later than 80; Salmon before 81; Jülicher between 100 and 180. A mid-second-century date, tying the intruders to followers of the teacher Carpocrates, was proposed by Pfleiderer and rejected by Bigg.

occasion.text: Jude had meant to write about the salvation they share, but found he must urge them instead to contend for the faith once delivered to the saints, because certain men had crept in unnoticed, turning God's grace into licence and denying the Lord.

themes.text: Things in threes. Mayor noted Jude's fondness for triplets: called, sanctified, preserved; mercy, peace, love; Israel, the angels, Sodom; defile, despise, speak evil; Cain, Balaam, Korah; separating, sensual, without the Spirit.

Kept. "Keep" comes five times. The angels who did not keep their place are kept for judgment, and the intruders are reserved for darkness; the faithful are preserved in Christ and told to keep themselves in God's love.
Ungodly. The "ungodly" family of words comes six times, four of them inside the prophecy of Enoch.
"These are…" Five times Jude points at the intruders with the word "these".

Sources beyond the Old Testament. Jude 14–15 quotes the prophecy of Enoch; R. H. Charles, editing 1 Enoch, judged that the whole of 1 Enoch 1:9 "has been quoted by Jude 14, 15 in a compressed form". Michael's dispute with the devil over the body of Moses (9) is not in the Old Testament; Origen said it came from the "Ascension of Moses", a book whose surviving text no longer contains the scene.

keyVerses.why: Contend for the faith once delivered to the saints.
The danger: grace turned into licence, and the Lord denied.
Michael's restraint: "The Lord rebuke thee."
The prophecy of Enoch, the seventh from Adam.
Build, pray, keep yourselves in the love of God.
The doxology: to him who is able to keep you from falling.

questions.question: Which James wrote the letter of James?

views.label: James the Lord's brother, a son of Joseph and Mary (the "Helvidian" view, after Helvidius, 4th century)
views.holders: J. B. Mayor (1892), who examines all three theories of the Lord's brothers

argument.text: The plain reading of Mark 6:3 and Matthew 13:55 names James as a brother of Jesus. Because the brothers did not believe in him during his ministry, they cannot have been among the Twelve; the risen Jesus appeared to James, and Paul calls him "the Lord's brother" and a "pillar" of the Jerusalem church.

views.label: The Lord's brother as a son of Joseph by an earlier marriage (the "Epiphanian" view, after Epiphanius, a 4th-century bishop)
views.holders: Examined by Mayor; Bigg reports that Clement of Alexandria held it of Jude, following the tradition in the Protevangelium of James; Eusebius says only that James was called the Lord's brother as a son of Joseph

argument.text: An early tradition that keeps the brothers as real family of Joseph's household while preserving Mary's virginity.

views.label: A cousin, the same man as James the son of Alphaeus, one of the Twelve (the "Hieronymian" view, after Jerome)
views.holders: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men ch. 2; Easton's Bible Dictionary (1897)

argument.text: "Brother" is read in the wider sense of kinsman: Jerome made James the son of a sister of the Lord's mother, which lets the writer be one of the apostles.

views.label: Undecided between the son of Alphaeus and a Jerusalem leader
views.holders: John Calvin (1551)

argument.text: Calvin thought the "pillar" of Galatians 2:9 was more likely the apostle, the son of Alphaeus, because he doubted a non-apostle would rank above apostles — but he declined to say which James wrote the letter.

views.label: A later writer using the name, or a Jewish work lightly made Christian
views.holders: Spitta (a Jewish treatise with "Jesus Christ" added at 1:1 and 2:1), as reported by the ISBE; Davidson, Hilgenfeld, Baur, Zeller, Hausrath, von Soden, Jülicher, Harnack and Bacon, who dated it between about 70 and 150

argument.text: The letter has little explicit Christian teaching and is written in good Greek.

questions.question: Who were the "brothers" of Jesus named in Mark 6:3 and Matthew 13:55?

views.label: Helvidian: younger children of Joseph and Mary
views.holders: Helvidius (4th century); J. B. Mayor (1892)

argument.text: The words are taken at their plain sense: James, Joses, Judas and Simon were sons of Mary born after Jesus.

views.label: Epiphanian: sons of Joseph by an earlier wife
views.holders: Epiphanius (4th century); Clement of Alexandria, as Bigg reports; examined by Mayor

argument.text: They were older half-brothers through Joseph, a tradition that keeps Mary a virgin.

views.label: Hieronymian: cousins
views.holders: Jerome (Hieronymus); Easton's Bible Dictionary (1897)

argument.text: "Brother" means kinsman: they were sons of a sister of the Lord's mother, and James is the same man as James the son of Alphaeus.

views.label: The brother of Jesus and of James
views.holders: J. B. Mayor (1907), Charles Bigg (1901), the ISBE

argument.text: The same family list names "James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon". Mayor thought Jude probably the youngest or next to youngest of the Lord's brothers. Eusebius, from Hegesippus, tells how the grandsons of Jude — who was said to have been the Lord's brother in the flesh — were brought before the emperor Domitian and released when they showed hands hardened by farm work.

views.label: The apostle "Judas of James", one of the Twelve
views.holders: Easton's Bible Dictionary (1897); Calvin treats Jude as an apostle

argument.text: Luke lists "Judas the brother of James" among the Twelve — apparently the man also called Thaddaeus or Lebbaeus. In the KJV the words "the brother" are supplied; the Greek has only "Judas of James", which can also mean "son of James".

views.label: A later Judas
views.holders: Grotius (Judas, a later bishop of Jerusalem); Harnack ("brother of James" added between 150 and 180); Jülicher (a writer from a circle that honoured James) — all as reported by Bigg

argument.text: These proposals follow from dating the letter in the second century; Bigg remarked that they rest on that assumption.

questions.question: Did the apostle Peter write 2 Peter?

views.label: Doubted from early times
views.holders: Origen; Eusebius; Jerome

argument.text: Origen spoke of one acknowledged letter of Peter and perhaps a second, which was doubtful. Eusebius said the second letter was not received as canonical, though many found it useful and read it with the other Scriptures. Jerome reported that many thought it was not Peter's because its style differs from the first, and elsewhere explained the difference by Peter's using two different interpreters.

views.label: Written by the apostle Peter
views.holders: Zahn (by Peter's own hand, before 1 Peter); Bigg (genuine, the style differing because Peter used different helpers); Easton (1897); the ISBE, citing Salmon, Warfield and Zahn

argument.text: The writer's own claims — the coming death the Lord had shown him, the voice on the holy mount, "this second epistle" — together with words shared with 1 Peter and the early Hebrew form of the name, "Symeon".

views.label: Peter's teaching, set down by a disciple at his command
views.holders: John Calvin (1551)

argument.text: Calvin did not recognise Peter's own language in it, but found nothing unworthy of Peter, and thought one of his disciples wrote it at his direction.

views.label: A later writer using Peter's name
views.holders: Chase (about AD 150), as reported by the ISBE; J. B. Mayor (1907)

argument.text: Weak early attestation, a style unlike 1 Peter, and dependence on Jude; Mayor also thought the phrase "the holy mount" pointed to a later stage of tradition. Even so, Hort — as Mayor recalls — said that if asked he would judge the balance of argument against the letter, and the moment he had done so would begin to think he might be wrong.

questions.question: Jude and 2 Peter share a run of the same material. Which came first?

views.label: Jude came first, and 2 Peter used it
views.holders: J. B. Mayor (1907), who lists Neander, Credner, Ewald, Hilgenfeld, Holtzmann, Harnack, Bernhard Weiss, Abbott, Farrar, Salmon and Chase; Bigg adds Reuss, Jülicher and von Soden. The ISBE allows that perhaps a majority favour it

argument.text: 2 Peter's unexplained remark about angels who bring no railing accusation reads like a riddle whose answer is Michael in Jude 9; "darkness reserved" suits Jude's wandering stars better than 2 Peter's wells; and 2 Peter drops Jude's material from Enoch. Mayor doubted that anyone would gather scattered phrases from 2 Peter to build Jude's tight cluster of images.

views.label: 2 Peter came first, and Jude used it
views.holders: Luther; Lumby, Mansel, Plummer, Spitta and Zahn (as listed by Bigg); Bigg himself; the ISBE, following Zahn. Döllinger held it and later gave it up

argument.text: 2 Peter speaks of false teachers still to come, Jude of men already present; Jude's "before of old ordained" and his call to remember the apostles' words may point back to 2 Peter; and the greater figure, Peter, is less likely to be the borrower.

views.label: A middle position
views.holders: Kühl, as reported by Bigg

argument.text: 2 Peter 2:1–3:2 is an insertion, taken from Jude, into an earlier letter that Jude had himself used. Bigg called this kind of solution a last resort.

views.label: Both drew on a common source
views.holders: Raised as a possibility and set aside by the ISBE

argument.text: The shared material would come from a third writing now lost; the ISBE notes that nothing from antiquity hints at one.

views.label: Rome, called Babylon as a figure
views.holders: Papias and Clement of Alexandria, as reported by Eusebius; Bigg, who says the view was universal until the Reformation and still the most common; Mayor; Grotius, Whitby, Lardner and others named in the note by Calvin's editor

argument.text: Revelation calls Rome "Babylon"; a strong tradition places Peter in Rome; and Mark and Silvanus are not known to have gone east.

views.label: Babylon on the Euphrates
views.holders: Calvin; Erasmus; Beza, John Lightfoot, Adam Clarke and others named by Calvin's editor; Easton (1897); the ISBE

argument.text: Peter writes plainly, and a figurative place-name in a greeting would be odd; many Jews lived there. Calvin's editor noted that dating a letter by a figurative name has no other example in Scripture.

views.label: Babylon in Egypt, a Roman fortress at what is now Old Cairo
views.holders: Bishop Pearson, Mill and Le Clerc, as reported by Bigg and Calvin's editor

argument.text: A real place of that name existed. Against it, Bigg notes that in the first century it was only a large military post.

views.label: Jerusalem (or Joppa)
views.holders: Harnack ("possibly Rome, but more probably Jerusalem"); others mentioned by Bigg

argument.text: A figurative name for the city that rejected Christ.

questions.question: When Peter wrote "by Silvanus", was Silvanus the carrier or the secretary?

views.label: The bearer of the letter
views.holders: The ISBE; Hort, who traces Silvanus's journey through the five regions

argument.text: The phrase most naturally names the man who carried the letter to its readers.

views.label: A secretary who shaped the Greek
views.holders: Bigg; Zahn, as Bigg reports

argument.text: If Peter used a helper to draft one letter, he likely did so as a rule — which would explain why 1 and 2 Peter read so differently.

questions.question: Why does Jude quote the Book of Enoch, which is not in the Old Testament?

views.label: He quoted one true prophecy without endorsing the whole book
views.holders: The ISBE

argument.text: Just as Paul quoted Greek poets without endorsing them, Jude could cite a saying he took to be true.

views.label: One of several New Testament uses of Jewish tradition
views.holders: J. B. Mayor (1907)

argument.text: Mayor set it beside other details taken from Jewish tradition rather than the Old Testament text, such as the three and a half years of Elijah's drought in James 5:17.

views.label: A reason to doubt the letter
views.holders: Many in Jerome's day, as he reports

argument.text: Jerome wrote that many rejected Jude because it quotes the apocryphal Enoch, though by age and use it had gained authority and was counted among the Scriptures.

questions.question: When were these four letters written?

views.label: James: the 40s AD, before the Jerusalem council
views.holders: Mayor; Schaff; Plumptre, Alford, Zahn, Dods and others listed by the ISBE

argument.text: No Gentile question and no circumcision debate; no mention of the fall of Jerusalem.

views.label: James: about 60–62, late in James's life
views.holders: Easton; Wiesinger, Farrar and others listed by the ISBE

argument.text: Settled congregations, and the Lord's coming has been delayed long enough to call for patience.

views.label: James: after his death, AD 70–150
views.holders: Baur, Harnack, Jülicher, Bacon and others listed by the ISBE

argument.text: Good Greek, little explicit Christian doctrine, and a supposed reaction to Paul.

views.label: 1 Peter: AD 58–64, before Nero's persecution
views.holders: Bigg

argument.text: Hostility from neighbours, but no persecution by the state yet.

views.label: 1 Peter: about AD 64, under Nero
views.holders: The ISBE

argument.text: Everything in the letter is read as pointing to Nero's time.

views.label: 1 Peter: AD 83–93, not by Peter
views.holders: Harnack, as reported by Bigg

argument.text: Paul's influence and the lack of personal detail.

views.label: 2 Peter: about AD 60–63
views.holders: Zahn, as reported by Bigg

argument.text: Written by Peter himself, before 1 Peter.

views.label: 2 Peter: shortly before Peter's death, mid-60s
views.holders: Easton; the ISBE; Calvin

argument.text: The writer says his death is near.

views.label: 2 Peter: about AD 150, or later
views.holders: Chase, as reported by the ISBE; Mayor, who weighed several second-century dates

argument.text: Weak early attestation and dependence on Jude.

views.label: Jude: about 65 to 80
views.holders: Bigg (not much after 65); Easton (66 or 70); Zahn (70–75); Mayor and Lumby (about 80); Chase (not later than 80); Salmon (before 81)

argument.text: Zahn read verse 5 as a sign that Jerusalem had already fallen.

views.label: Jude: AD 100–180
views.holders: Jülicher, as reported by Bigg; Pfleiderer argued for the mid-second century, which Bigg rejected

argument.text: The intruders are taken to be second-century teachers.

questions.question: James says that "by works a man is justified, and not by faith only"; Paul says "justified by faith without the deeds of the law". How do the two fit?

views.label: James is correcting a misuse of Paul's teaching, not Paul himself
views.holders: The general belief in the Church from Augustine onward, as Mayor describes it

argument.text: James aims at followers who stretched Paul's words into an excuse for faith without deeds.

views.label: They use "justify" in two senses
views.holders: John Calvin (1551); Easton (1897); Alfred Plummer (1891); the ISBE

argument.text: Paul means being counted righteous before God; James means faith proved real before others by what it does. Plummer saw no opposition between them, and the ISBE spoke of the same truth seen from opposite sides.

views.label: Justification grows through good works
views.holders: The Council of Trent, Session 6 (1547), Decree on Justification, ch. X

argument.text: The justified, with faith working together with good works, increase in the righteousness they have received through Christ's grace and are justified further — and the decree cites James 2:24 for it.

views.label: The two contradict each other
views.holders: F. C. Baur, Renan and Weiffenbach, who held that James attacks Paul directly (as reported by Schaff)

argument.text: James's "not by faith only" is read as a reply aimed at Paul. Schaff adds that Luther sharpened the contrast by translating Romans 3:28 with "alone" (allein).

views.label: James wrote first, without Paul in view
views.holders: J. B. Mayor (1892); Philip Schaff (1889); Neander and Bishop Lightfoot, as Mayor reports

argument.text: James wrote before the Jerusalem council and had no reference to Paul; Mayor went further and thought Paul later wrote with James's phrases in mind. Both writers use Abraham and quote Genesis 15:6, but James also points to the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22), and Paul stresses that Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised.

canon.label: Muratorian Fragment
canon.who: An early Latin list of New Testament books

claim.text: This early list receives Jude among the church's books; James and the two letters of Peter are not named. Its date is debated: most put it about 170, Salmon and Zahn about 200–210.
Eusebius reports that Clement's Outlines commented on the disputed books, naming Jude and the other Catholic letters. Which of the other letters he covered is not certain.
Origen treats 1 Peter as acknowledged and calls a second letter doubtful. He is the first writer known to cite James by name as Scripture, and he uses Jude.

canon.label: Syriac Peshitta (date debated, 2nd–4th century)
canon.who: The Bible of the Syriac-speaking churches

claim.text: The Syriac New Testament includes James and 1 Peter but leaves out 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation. When it was made is debated; it is placed here only for order.

Eusebius sorts the books into accepted and disputed. 1 Peter is accepted; James, Jude and 2 Peter are disputed though recognised by many. He says few of the ancients mention James or Jude, yet both have been read publicly in very many churches. As Plummer sets it out, 2 Peter was doubted as to who wrote it, James and Jude as to whether they were apostolic.
Cyril includes James among the books of the New Testament.
Athanasius lists seven Catholic letters: one of James, two of Peter, three of John and one of Jude.

Jerome accepts all four but records the doubts: many thought 2 Peter was not Peter's because of its different style; some claimed James was published by someone else under his name; and many rejected Jude for quoting Enoch, though by age and use it had gained authority. He included 2 Peter in his Latin Bible, the Vulgate.

canon.label: Third Council of Carthage
canon.who: A council of North African bishops

claim.text: The council's list includes James and 2 Peter. Only those two are named in the sources read here; the full list was not checked.

At the Reformation Erasmus and Cajetan revived the old doubts about James, and Erasmus rejected 2 Peter. Schaff dates Erasmus's annotated Greek New Testament to 1516 and his Paraphrase to 1522, and Cajetan's commentary on the epistles to 1531.

In the preface to his first edition, Luther called James "a right strawy Epistle" by comparison with other books, "for it has no character of the Gospel in it", and placed Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation at the end of his New Testament. He did not hold James to be any apostle's writing, and judged Jude a copy of 2 Peter. The "straw" sentence was left out of later editions. Westcott dates the preface to the first edition of 1522; Schaff gives 1524.
Calvin comments on all four as Scripture, though he thought 2 Peter was probably written down by a disciple at Peter's command.

parallels.title: Jude and 2 Peter side by side

pairs.note: Greetings "be multiplied".
"All diligence".
Intruders who deny the Lord; their condemnation long prepared.
Reminding readers of what they already know (compare also 2 Pet 3:1).
Sinning angels kept in darkness for judgment.
Sodom and Gomorrah set out as an example.
Defiling the flesh, despising authority, speaking evil of dignities.
No "railing accusation" — Michael by name in Jude, unnamed angels in 2 Peter.
Speaking evil of what they do not understand, like brute beasts.
The way of Balaam, for pay.
Blots at the community's feasts.
Clouds without water (Jude) and wells without water (2 Peter), driven by wind.
Darkness reserved for ever.
"Great swelling words".
Remember the apostles' words: mockers or scoffers in the last time, walking after their own lusts.
Kept without fault and from falling (see also 2 Pet 3:17, "lest ye… fall").
The closing doxology.

claim.text: Seventeen points where the two letters run together, following Mayor's walk through them in order; Bigg discusses the same pairs. The heart of the overlap is Jude 4–18 beside 2 Peter 2:1–3:3. Only Jude has the prophecy of Enoch, Michael and the body of Moses by name, Cain and Korah, the wandering stars and the wilderness generation; only 2 Peter has Noah's flood, Lot, Balaam's speaking ass, the dog and the sow, the transfiguration, the scoffers' question and Paul's letters. The grouping of the pairs into four kinds is ours.

parallels.title: James and the Sermon on the Mount

pairs.note: Joy under persecution, with the prophets as example (see also Jas 1:2).
Be perfect.
Ask, and it shall be given (see also Jas 4:2–3).
Good gifts from the Father.
The righteousness of God.
Hearers and doers.
The whole law kept: guilty of all for one point; the least commandment (see also Jas 1:25).
Saying without doing (see also Jas 2:14–26).
The poor inherit the kingdom.
Mercy for the merciful (see also Matt 6:14–15).
Daily food, daily bread (Mayor, following Chase).
Known by their fruit: figs, olives, grapes.
Peacemakers.
Two loyalties are impossible.
A pure, undivided heart (see also Jas 1:8 and Matt 6:22).
Do not judge (see also Jas 5:9).
Tomorrow.
Moth and rust.
No oaths; let yes be yes and no be no — the ISBE calls this the exact parallel.
Grass that withers.
The way that leads to death or to life.

claim.text: Twenty-one echoes of Matthew 5–7 in James, from Mayor's verse-by-verse list; the ISBE counts "at least ten". Mayor stresses that the closeness "never amounts to actual quotation" — it is like the remembered sayings of a teacher sinking into a hearer's heart. Where a row has a second James passage it is named in the note. Mayor also lists echoes outside the Sermon — James 1:6 with Matthew 21:21, 2:8 with 22:39, 4:10 with 23:12, 5:9 with 24:33, and 2:5, 4:9 and 5:1 with Luke 6:20–25 — which fall outside this chart. His marks for the strongest parallels are not shown, because the scan's text garbles them.

pairs.note: Readers in the dispersion, "scattered abroad".
Trials of many kinds and the testing of your faith.
Grass and flower — both drawing on Isaiah 40:6–7.
A crown: of life in James, of glory in 1 Peter.
Born or begotten by the word.
Put away evil and receive the word.
"God resisteth the proud" — Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek Old Testament form.
Resist the devil.
Humble yourselves, and he will lift you up.
Covering a multitude of sins — Proverbs 10:12.

claim.text: Ten places where James and 1 Peter share wording or an Old Testament text. Mayor argued that 1 Peter borrowed from James; the ISBE notes that it has been ably argued the other way about.

timelines.title: James, the Lord's brother, in the story

events.label: Named among Jesus' brothers at Nazareth
The brothers do not yet believe in him
The risen Jesus is seen by James
The brothers gather with the disciples
Paul meets "James the Lord's brother" in Jerusalem
Freed from prison, Peter says "Go shew these things unto James"
James gives the deciding speech at the Jerusalem meeting
Paul reports to James on his last visit to Jerusalem
The letter of James
Stoned at the order of the high priest Ananus, by Josephus's account — usually dated AD 62. Hegesippus, quoted by Eusebius, remembers him as James the Just

claim.text: The steps follow the order of the New Testament story; they are a sequence, not dates. Paul also names James as one of the three "pillars" of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 2:9). Where the letter falls in it depends on which James wrote it and when — both disputed. Jerome says James led the Jerusalem church for thirty years, until the seventh year of Nero.

events.label: A Bethsaida fisherman, brought to Jesus by Andrew and named Cephas
Called from his nets to become a fisher of men
Confesses Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God
With James and John at the Transfiguration
Denies knowing Jesus three times
The risen Lord appears to him, then bids him: "Feed my sheep"
Preaches to the crowds at Pentecost
Brings the gospel to the centurion Cornelius and his household
Paul names him a pillar, then opposes him at Antioch
Writes to believers scattered across Asia Minor
By tradition, crucified at Rome under Nero

claim.text: The steps follow the order of the New Testament story, not dates, from the Galilean fisherman to the letter to Asia Minor; Jesus foretells the manner of Peter's death (John 21:18–19), but that it came at Rome under Nero is later tradition, as Eusebius reports it, and is labelled so.

timelines.title: Jude, the Lord's brother, in the story

events.label: Named among Jesus' brothers at Nazareth
The brothers do not yet believe in him
The brothers gather in prayer with the apostles
The Lord's brothers travel with their wives; Mayor counts Jude among them
Writes as "brother of James" (Mayor, Bigg and the ISBE take him for the Lord's brother; others doubt it)
By tradition, his grandsons are questioned by the emperor Domitian

claim.text: The steps follow the order of the New Testament story, not dates, and most speak of the Lord's brothers as a group; the last comes from Hegesippus as Eusebius reports it, and is labelled as tradition.

maps.title: The five regions of 1 Peter's readers

stops.name: Pontus
stops.note: North-east Asia Minor, along the Black Sea. Its western coast was joined to Bithynia as one Roman province. People from Pontus were at Pentecost (Acts 2:9), and Aquila was born there (Acts 18:2).

stops.name: Galatia
stops.note: Central Asia Minor; a Roman province from 25 BC, its capital Ancyra (modern Ankara). Paul's churches of Galatia were here.

stops.name: Cappadocia
stops.note: East-central Asia Minor, the easternmost and largest province; a province from AD 17, its chief city Caesarea. Cappadocians were at Pentecost.

stops.name: Asia
stops.note: Western Asia Minor on the Aegean, a Roman province from 133 BC with Ephesus as capital; home of the seven churches of Revelation. People from Asia were at Pentecost.

stops.name: Bithynia
stops.note: North-west Asia Minor, on the Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara. The Spirit kept Paul from entering it (Acts 16:7); early in the 2nd century its Roman governor Pliny wrote to the emperor Trajan about the many Christians brought before him.

claim.text: 1 Peter names its readers' regions in the order Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, Bithynia — though Pontus and Bithynia were one Roman province, they stand at opposite ends of the list. Hort took the order to follow the route of the man carrying the letter; Easton thought it the order that would occur to someone writing from Babylon on the Euphrates. Bigg notes that, read loosely, the list covers the whole of Asia Minor except the south coast. Pins mark the site's region centres, not boundaries.

stops.name: Babylon on the Euphrates
stops.note: The literal city: the view of Calvin, Erasmus, Easton and the ISBE, among others.

stops.name: Rome, called Babylon
stops.note: The figurative reading reported by Eusebius from Papias and Clement of Alexandria, which Bigg calls the most common.

claim.text: Where 1 Peter was written depends on what "Babylon" means. These are the two main candidates in the site's place data; a Babylon in Egypt and Jerusalem have also been proposed (see the question on Babylon).

stops.name: Pontus
stops.note: Hort thought Silvanus probably landed at Sinope, a port on the Black Sea coast (not in this site's place data, so the region is shown).

stops.name: Galatia
stops.note: Inland to Ancyra, the capital of Galatia.

stops.name: Cappadocia
stops.note: On to Caesarea, almost the only large town in Cappadocia.

stops.name: Asia
stops.note: West along the great road to Ephesus through Apamea, then north through Asia.

stops.name: Bithynia
stops.note: At length into Bithynia, to take ship there or return to where he landed — completing the circuit.

claim.text: Hort argued that the order of the regions in 1 Peter 1:1 is not chance but traces the journey of Silvanus, who carried the letter: landing on the Black Sea coast, going inland through Galatia and Cappadocia, west to Asia, and north to Bithynia to close the circuit. Bigg found the route probable. The towns Hort names are not in the site's place data, so the line joins the region centres and is only a sketch of his route.

nodes.label: James
nodes.note: "The Lord's brother" (Gal 1:19), leader of the Jerusalem church; linked with the letter of James.

nodes.label: Juda (Judas)
nodes.note: "Juda" in Mark, "Judas" in Matthew. Whether he is the Jude of the letter is a separate question.

nodes.label: Jude's grandsons
nodes.note: Brought before the emperor Domitian and released, as Eusebius tells it from Hegesippus.

edges.label: "brother of James" (if he is the Jude of the letter)

claim.text: Mark and Matthew name four "brethren" of Jesus: James, Joses, Juda (Judas) and Simon. The relationship has been read three ways — as younger children of Joseph and Mary (the Helvidian view), as sons of Joseph by an earlier wife (the Epiphanian view), or as cousins (the Hieronymian view, after Jerome). The lines here say only "brother", as the text does.

flows.title: Where the Old Testament comes from

claim.text: Each line runs from an Old Testament book to the letter that draws on it; its width is the number of Old Testament passages the letter quotes or alludes to from that book, counting quotations and clear allusions together, from the checked lists on this page. Isaiah and Psalms dominate 1 Peter. Easton counted about thirty-five Old Testament references in 1 Peter and eleven in 2 Peter, so a fuller list would add fainter allusions. Jude's sources outside the Old Testament — 1 Enoch and the lost Assumption of Moses — are not shown.
